status_detail: Multi-league fantasy football tools. Every tool lives under /l/[leagueId] with leagues auto-discovered from Sleeper and format detected from settings.type (including type 3, which is Sleeper's undocumented guillotine code). Four live leagues: Dah Dynasty League (dynasty, in season), 2026 Half PPR (redraft, drafts Sep 7), Sunday Scaries #2 (redraft, full PPR, in season), and Dah Chopped League (guillotine, 16 teams, $1000 FAAB, still pre-draft). Guillotine leagues get a weekly FAAB advisor at /l/[id]/faab, /api/faab and a Tuesday email. Written playbooks with sources at /strategy. His rankings moved off Substack to the FantasyPros platform on 2026-09-17 and are read from there by week rather than by post, per scoring, so each league finally reads a list in its own scoring. SURVIVOR is a live recommendation engine at /survivor and /api/survivor: no-vig moneylines from ESPN, real public pick percentages from Yahoo, first-place equity scoring and a season-long Hungarian assignment for future value. TWO POOLS now, 500 entries and 30, tracked apart: separate burned teams, separate logged distributions, separate chalk factors, one shared data pull. Switcher on the page, ?pool=<id>|all on the API, one labelled card per pool in the Thursday email. Each pool carries a POSTURE, computed from expected entries alive at week 18, which breaks ties toward safety in a pool that will thin to one entry and toward leverage in one that will split. Week 1 live: 500 pool takes JAX, 30 pool takes LAC. A PULSE now keeps it current: /api/pulse called every fifteen minutes by GitHub Actions, tiered by the Eastern clock (live gameday, hourly, overnight), plus five scheduled emails through one shell and a Sunday 11:45 exception alarm that stays silent when nothing is wrong.

2026-09-22 (late, 3): The bid model was bidding its ceiling on everything. raw = market x urgency x value x quality meant the card offered what a player was WORTH rather than what it takes to WIN him, which is how a room whose six observed multiweek bids average $56 got a $106 recommendation on Joe Burrow. Split in two: worthToMe (market x urgency x value factor x quality x play probability) is the walk-away, takesToWin (market x demand pressure x posture edge, 1.15 red / 1.08 yellow / 1.0 green) is the bid, and the bid is capped by the lower of the two. Demand pressure is now bidders per comparable player rather than a bidder count: contestedBy counts only rivals who would start him AND hold at least the tier's market price, comparableSupply counts available players at the position within 2 projected points. Week 3 had 4 startable QBs against 2 needy rosters, so the QB chain repriced from $106/$103/$98/$37 to $59/$58/$58/$38 with walk-aways of $107/$99/$99/$56, while Puka Nacua held at $194 because 12 rivals would start him and nothing comparable is left. Worst case $299 to $253. Reason lines now name the rival (DonovanQ) and say how many comparable players he could buy instead.

(2) Injury: a player whose status is Out/IR/PUP/doubtful now contributes zero weekly gain, loses the urgency multiplier entirely (urgency is about needing help Sunday) and takes a posture-keyed discount (red 0.3, yellow 0.45, green 0.7). (3) Demand: the report now computes each surviving rival's weakest starter per position and counts how many would start a given player; 3+ pays 1.15x, zero pays 0.85x, and the reason line says so. This is the first time the model has known anything about rival NEED rather than just rival money. (4) The researched hold rule (both docs: do not pay 10-20% of budget for 2-3 points) is now a rate ceiling of 10% of the original budget per 3 points of weekly gain, floored at 2%, lifted only for a championship-tier buy in a green week. Chains now sort by bid rather than by gain, since Sleeper processes highest first and the two orders can now disagree. BudgetPlan gained originalBudget. notes.note: REFRESH CADENCE QUESTION TURNED UP TWO REAL BUGS. Jack asked whether injuries, news and pick percentages update weekly and said they should be daily. (1) SILENT PARTIAL FETCH. getSeasonGames caught a failed week and substituted an empty array, then cached all eighteen weeks for fifteen minutes including the hole. A missing FUTURE week quietly rewrites every burn cost; a missing CURRENT week makes currentWeek() skip ahead, so the page would have shown next week's board and invited a pick for the wrong slate. That is the worst failure this tool can have and nothing would have looked wrong. There is now cachedWithFallback in lib/redis/cached.ts: it keeps a seven-day last-known-good copy, validates completeness (all 18 weeks present, a Yahoo week covering 24+ teams, a non-empty injury list) rather than only catching throws, serves the last good copy on a short retry TTL when a fetch is short or fails, never overwrites a good copy with a bad one, and reports staleness so the page says so out loud instead of passing yesterday's numbers off as today's. Per-week fetches also retry once. The redis client is now built lazily behind a Proxy so the module is importable without env, which is what makes the fallback logic testable against an in-memory store. (2) YAHOO ONLY PUBLISHES THE CURRENT WEEK. The response carries a key for all 22 weeks, which is where the earlier and wrong claim of 'all 22 weeks of data' came from, but the future ones are empty arrays and past weeks drop off. That silently broke the calibration shipped an hour earlier: it fits the pool against the PUBLIC baseline for the weeks already played, and come Week 2 that baseline would have been gone, so alpha would have stayed at 1 forever with no error anywhere. Each week's public distribution is now archived to survivor:public-archive:2026 the first time it is seen, never expired, with live numbers merged over the top so the week in progress stays fresh and forgotten weeks are kept. Writes are skipped for drift under 0.05 percentage points. 28 new tests, 353 green.

SURVIVOR LEARNS FROM THE POOL NOW. Jack corrected two assumptions in the first build. He cannot see his pool's pick percentages until the week is OVER, which made the live paste box dead weight, and the pool also shows WHICH TEAMS THE FIELD HAS USED, which the research had flagged as the input that decides late-season weeks and which the first build ignored entirely. Both are now the same one-paste-a-week loop. THE PASTE IS RETROSPECTIVE: after a week ends he pastes what the pool picked, and that single input does three jobs. (1) It fits a CHALK FACTOR, one parameter, q_pool proportional to q_public^alpha, where above 1 means his pool crowds the favourite harder than the public does; it is fitted by golden-section search against Yahoo's distribution for those same past weeks and shrunk toward 1 by sample size, because one week is a coincidence and not a tendency (a single observation moves it only a third of the way). (2) It DERIVES THE BURNED MAP: the fraction of surviving entries carrying each team, which then scales that team's projected ownership, so a team 80% of the field has used reads as nearly unpickable by them. (3) It DERIVES ENTRIES ALIVE, because survivors equals entries times the share of the field on teams that won, so the number Jack was told to maintain by hand last session is now computed and the manual field is only a pre-season fallback. Invariant worth keeping: burned sums to exactly the number of weeks logged, since every survivor has used one team per completed week, and that is a test. Weeks whose results are not all in are refused rather than guessed, and a week where the entire field busted is treated as unscoreable rather than dividing by zero. The engine now takes Yahoo's WHOLE 22-week blob rather than one week's slice, because past weeks are the public baseline the calibration compares against; without them there is nothing to fit. Candidates carry a leverage flag when a big share of the field can no longer follow them onto a team. Also confirmed for the record: future schedule was already the core of the engine, the Hungarian solve runs on all 18 weeks of real moneylines, not ratings. 63 new tests, 325 green. SURVIVOR REBUILT FROM A CHASSIS INTO AN ENGINE. It had been pool config, checkboxes and six essays, with hardcoded 2026 power ratings and three phases of 'coming soon'. Jack asked for it to run itself and stay current on public pick percentages. Researched the format first (Bergman & Imbrogno's sequential-assignment paper, PoolGenius on expected value and pool size, the standard de-vig and spread-to-margin conversions) and then went looking for data, which is where the two findings that shaped everything came from. YAHOO PUBLISHES REAL PICK PERCENTAGES FREE: the Survival Football pick-distribution page ships all 32 teams for all 22 weeks as a JSON blob embedded in the HTML, unauthenticated, so ownership is real submitted picks rather than a model's forecast of them. ESPN'S SCOREBOARD CARRIES MONEYLINES: every 2026 week 1-18 is priced with DraftKings moneylines and spreads, no key and no quota, which retires the-odds-api item that had been sitting in next_steps since August. SLEEPER CANNOT BE READ: the pool is not in the public API (every pick'em endpoint 404s) and lives behind sleeper.com/graphql, which answers unauthorized without a session token; that was offered and declined in favour of one-tap logging, because a token that expires silently on a Saturday night is worse than five seconds a week. FOUR IDEAS DO THE WORK. (1) Equity, not safety: M = p(1-(1-r)^N)/r, where r is the fraction of RIVALS surviving given your pick wins. The common p/q shortcut is only correct if the whole field is split across your one game, and overstates leverage badly on a real slate. (2) De-vigged moneylines, always: -185 reads as 64.9% raw and 64.3% fair, and that gap compounds over 18 weeks. (3) Future value as a shadow price: the season is an assignment problem (one team per week, none twice, maximise total log survival) solved with a Hungarian implementation, and burn cost is how much the best path worsens without that team. (4) Both answers on screen: highest equity and safest board are shown side by side, because the engine will sometimes sell safety and Jack should see the price. VERIFIED AGAINST THE REAL WEEK 1 SLATE BEFORE ANY UI EXISTED, which caught two bugs no unit test would have. Future cost came back 0.000 for almost every team, and the cause was structural rather than a coding error: over an 8-week window you only need 8 of 32 teams, so removing any one never changes the optimum and the shadow price is always zero. It now solves the whole remaining season, which is a constraint that actually binds, with the published preference for a short horizon preserved by the discount weight instead (0.8 per week puts 2% on week seventeen). And the injury filter was WR and RB wide, so every single candidate carried three or four injury flags, which is the same as carrying none; it is quarterbacks and tackles now, two per card. A third bug was found by a bad test fixture and was real: a partial ownership snapshot had its missing mass spread over the few unlisted teams, inventing 31% ownership out of nothing, so coverage below half now degrades to an explicitly uniform field and says so. FOUR IDEAS DO THE WORK. (1) Elimination risk is a probability, not a rank: 20k Monte Carlo draws over every alive team's projected score, so the answer is 'you carry 12.5% against a 6.25% baseline' rather than 'you are 12th'. (2) A player is worth what he adds to your STARTING lineup, so the solver refuses to sell you a 9.4 tight end when your flex already starts a 9.4. (3) Pacing runs on eliminations remaining, not the calendar, because the published month-by-month curve was written for an 18-team league running to December and this one reaches the endgame around week 11. (4) Claims are grouped into chains that all drop the SAME player, making them mutually exclusive, because four independent claims that each look reasonable can all land and cost four times what you meant to spend.
